claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has been produced in a hierarchical heterostructured state featuring multilevel chemical fluctuations.

Integrating imaging-derived microstructural descriptors into a physics-informed machine-learning model calibrated with targeted experiments will improve prediction of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness.
The proposed framework will predict the mechanical properties more rapidly than conventional simulation-based methods.
High-resolution TEM or SEM data can be used to quantify relevant microstructural descriptors for this alloy.
A limited set of high-fidelity tensile and fracture experiments can adequately calibrate the proposed model.
Grain-boundary character, local chemical fluctuations, and phase distributions capture the alloy’s hierarchical heterogeneity.
The extracted microstructural descriptors mediate or determine the measured mechanical response.
Direct measurement of governing microstructural features can establish robust structure–property correlations.
Embedding known physical relationships in the machine-learning model will improve its predictive performance.
The proposed approach circumvents the computational burden of full-scale simulations.
The method will reduce prediction error by approximately 15–20% relative to traditional thermophysical-parameter, CALPHAD, and first-principles approaches.
The method will improve computational efficiency by approximately two- to three-fold relative to the stated traditional approaches.
The framework may become unreliable when imaging resolution is insufficient to capture critical microstructural features.
The framework may become unreliable when the tested hierarchical structure differs substantially from structures represented in the training data.
Unanticipated phase changes may place samples outside the reliable domain of the model.
The magnitude of the accuracy and efficiency gains depends on imaging quality and training-data representativeness.
